1.note: The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. See how you translated **saying** in [1:1](ta:01).

2.note: Yahweh is using **on which a yoke has not gone up** as a common expression of the culture to mean “which has never been used for work.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [which has never been used for work]

2.q: לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר דַּבֵּ֣ר אֶל־בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל וְ⁠יִקְח֣וּ אֵלֶי⁠ךָ֩
2.note: If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate this so that there is not a quotation within a quotation. Alternate translation: [He told Moses and Aaron to tell the sons of Israel that they should bring to them]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a statute that is characterized by the law. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [is a legal statute]

3.note: The pronoun he refers to an indefinite person who will perform the slaughtering, while the pronoun his refers to Eleazar. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and someone shall slaughter it before Eleazar’s face]
Here, **his face** represents his presence. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [before him]

4.note: Here, **the face of the tent of meeting** represents the front of the tent of meeting. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [toward the front of the tent of meeting]

5.note: The pronoun **he** refers to an indefinite person, not to Eleazar. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And someone shall burn the cow]
Here, **his eyes** represents his sight. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [while he watches]

If it would be more natural in your language, you may want to put the information about the burning before the list of the cow’s parts. Alternate translation: [he shall burn its skin and its flesh and its blood and its dung]

The implication is that this list refers to the entirety of the cow. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [its skin and its flesh and its blood, and its dung—the entire cow]

6.note: Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe **wood** that is characterized by **cedar**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [cedar wood]

A **hyssop** is a kind of small, bushy plant with aromatic leaves. If your readers would not be familiar with what a hyssop is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and marjoram]

The **scarlet of worm** is a kind of crimson-dyed thread, with the dye being made from crushed scale insects. If your readers would not be familiar with what scarlet of worm is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [and scarlet thread]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **burning**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the fire burning the cow]

7.q: וְ⁠כִבֶּ֨ס בְּגָדָ֜י⁠ו הַ⁠כֹּהֵ֗ן וְ⁠רָחַ֤ץ בְּשָׂר⁠וֹ֙ בַּ⁠מַּ֔יִם וְ⁠אַחַ֖ר יָב֣וֹא אֶל־הַֽ⁠מַּחֲנֶ֑ה וְ⁠טָמֵ֥א הַ⁠כֹּהֵ֖ן עַד־הָ⁠עָֽרֶב׃
7.note: The priest’s coming to the camp did not happen right after the burning of the cow. The word **afterward** shows that he first needed to wash his clothes and bathe. Your language may have a connecting phrase that you can use to show this. Alternate translation: [After the priest washes his clothes and bathes his flesh in the water, he may come to the camp. The priest will be unclean until the evening.]

Yahweh is using **his flesh** to represent the priest’s whole body. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [himself]

8.note: Yahweh is not referring to a specific person by the phrase **the one burning it**. He means anyone who performs this task. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [Anyone who burns it]
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:7. Alternate translation: [himself]

9.note: Here Yahweh is speaking as if the Israelites were literally the **sons** of the patriarch Israel. He means that they are his descendants. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the descendants of Israel]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **keeping**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [to keep]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **impurity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for water to cleanse those who are unclean]

Here, the word translated impurity could refer to: (1) the quality of being unclean. In this case, the water is meant to be used to make pure things that are impure. Alternate translation: [for water to be used in cases of impurity] or [for water to cleanse impurity] (2) the act of sprinkling. Alternate translation: [for water for sprinkling]

The **water of impurity** is a kind of ritual cleansing water made by mixing the ashes of the cow with fresh water. If your readers would not be familiar with what water of impurity is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [for water that removes impurity]

10.note: Yahweh is not referring to a specific person by the phrase **the one gathering the ashes of the cow**. He means anyone who gathers the ashes. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [anyone who gathers the ashes of the cow]

Here Yahweh is speaking as if the Israelites were literally the **sons** of the patriarch Israel. He means that they are his descendants. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for the descendants of Israel]

Yahweh is not referring to a specific **sojourner**. He means any foreigner who lives among the Israelites. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and for any foreigner who lives among them]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **statute** that is characterized by **eternity**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for a statute that lasts forever]

11.note:
# General Information:

The ideas of “clean” and “purify” represent being acceptable to God. The ideas of “unclean,” “defile,” “impurity,” and “uncleanness” represent not being acceptable to God.
Alternate translation: [the dead body of any person]

12.q: ה֣וּא יִתְחַטָּא־ב֞⁠וֹ בַּ⁠יּ֧וֹם הַ⁠שְּׁלִישִׁ֛י וּ⁠בַ⁠יּ֥וֹם הַ⁠שְּׁבִיעִ֖י יִטְהָ֑ר וְ⁠אִם־לֹ֨א יִתְחַטָּ֜א בַּ⁠יּ֧וֹם הַ⁠שְּׁלִישִׁ֛י וּ⁠בַ⁠יּ֥וֹם הַ⁠שְּׁבִיעִ֖י לֹ֥א יִטְהָֽר
12.note: Here, the phrase on the seventh day in both places could go with: (1) purify himself. In this case, the purification should happen twice, on day three and on day seven. Alternate translation: [He shall purify himself with it two times, on the third day and on the seventh day. Then he will be clean. And if he does not purify himself two times, on the third day and on the seventh day, he will not be clean] (2) be clean. In this case, the purification happens once, on day three, and the person is clean on day seven. Alternate translation: [He shall purify himself with it on the third day, and on the seventh day he will be clean. And if he does not purify himself on the third day, then on the seventh day he will not be clean]

12.q: ה֣וּא יִתְחַטָּא־ב֞⁠וֹ בַּ⁠יּ֧וֹם הַ⁠שְּׁלִישִׁ֛י וּ⁠בַ⁠יּ֥וֹם הַ⁠שְּׁבִיעִ֖י יִטְהָ֑ר וְ⁠אִם־לֹ֨א יִתְחַטָּ֜א בַּ⁠יּ֧וֹם הַ⁠שְּׁלִישִׁ֛י וּ⁠בַ⁠יּ֥וֹם הַ⁠שְּׁבִיעִ֖י לֹ֥א יִטְהָֽר
12.note: Yahweh uses the word **if** here to indicate a contrast between the positive result of purification and the negative result of failing to purify. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [He shall purify himself with it on the third day and on the seventh day, and he will be clean. But if he does not purify himself on the third day and on the seventh day, he will not be clean.]

The pronoun **He** refers to the person who touched a dead body, and the pronoun **it** refers to the purification water. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [He shall purify himself with the purification water]

13.note: The expression **shall be cut off from Israel** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the rest of the Israelites. Alternate translation: [the Israelites shall drive that person out from among them]

Yahweh is speaking as if the person being expelled from the community were being physically **cut off**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And that person shall be expelled from Israel]

The expression **was not sprinkled on him** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [no one sprinkled the water of impurity on him]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because the water of impurity was not splashed on him]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **uncleanness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [he has not yet become clean]
See how you translated this phrase in 19:9.

14.note: Yahweh is presenting a possible condition, that a man dies in a tent, and everyone who comes to the tent or is in the tent will be unclean. Use a natural form in your language for introducing a condition that could happen. It may be helpful to reorder this sentence so that the conditional statement is first. Alternate translation: [if a man dies in a tent]

15.note: The expression **opened** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And every vessel that is open]

Yahweh is using the possessive form to describe a **cover** that is characterized by **cord**. If a speaker of your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [cover tied with cord]

16.note: Here, **the face of the field** represents “the surface of the open land.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the surface of the open land]

Here, **sword** represents “the means by which someone was killed.” If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [one who was killed]

17.note: The pronoun **they** refers to people in general, not to specific individuals. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And someone shall take]

Yahweh is using the adjective **unclean** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [for the person who is unclean]

The pronoun **he** refers to the person preparing the purification water, and the pronoun **it** refers to the dust of the sin offering. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and that person shall put living water on the dust]

Yahweh is using **living water** as a common expression of the culture to mean “flowing, fresh water.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [flowing water]

18.note: The pronoun **he** refers to the clean man who will perform the sprinkling. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the clean man shall sprinkle on the tent]

A **hyssop** is a kind of small, bushy plant. If your readers would not be familiar with what **hyssop** is, you could use the name of a similar plant that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [a small, bushy plant]

19.note: Yahweh is using the adjectives **clean** and **unclean** as nouns to mean certain kinds of people. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate these adjectives with equivalent phrases. Alternate translation: [And the clean person shall sprinkle on the unclean person]

The pronoun **he** refers to the person who was purified, not to the one who performed the sprinkling. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [and the unclean person shall wash his clothes and bathe in the water]

Here, the pronoun him refers to the unclean one. The pronoun he could refer to: (1) the clean one. In this case, the phrase refers to the clean person sprinkling the water on the unclean person. Alternate translation: [And the clean one shall purify the unclean one] (2) the unclean one. In this case, the phrase indicates that the unclean person must successfully complete the ritual to become clean. Alternate translation: [And the unclean one shall purify himself]

20.note: The expression **shall be cut off from the midst of the assembly** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is the rest of the Israelites. Alternate translation: [the rest of the Israelites shall drive that person out from the midst of the assembly]

Yahweh is speaking as if the person being expelled from the community were being physically **cut off**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [shall be expelled from the assembly]

See how you translated the similar expression in 19:13. The expression **was not splashed on him** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [No one splashed the water of impurity on him]

See how you translated the similar expression in 19:13. If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **impurity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Water that makes people clean]

20.q: וְ⁠אִ֤ישׁ אֲשֶׁר־יִטְמָא֙ וְ⁠לֹ֣א יִתְחַטָּ֔א וְ⁠נִכְרְתָ֛ה הַ⁠נֶּ֥פֶשׁ הַ⁠הִ֖וא מִ⁠תּ֣וֹךְ הַ⁠קָּהָ֑ל כִּי֩ & מִקְדַּ֨שׁ יְהוָ֜ה טִמֵּ֗א מֵ֥י נִדָּ֛ה לֹא־זֹרַ֥ק עָלָ֖י⁠ו טָמֵ֥א הֽוּא
20.note: The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [Because he has made the holy place of Yahweh unclean]

21.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **eternity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for a statute that lasts forever]

Yahweh is using **a statute of eternity** as a common expression of the culture to mean “a permanent rule.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [for a lasting regulation]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **impurity**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [the water used to cleanse the unclean]

22.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 19:17. Moses is using the adjective **unclean** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [the person who is unclean]

Here, Yahweh could be referring to touching: (1) any object that the unclean person has touched. Alternate translation: [touching something that the unclean one has touched] (2) the unclean person. Alternate translation: [touching the unclean one]
